articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously appointed Frederick W. Shavies II as the city’s next Chief of Police at its regular meeting on Monday, July 7. Shavies, who began his tenure on July 22, brings nearly two decades of law enforcement experience and most recently served as Deputy Chief of Police in Oakland. Widely respected for his strategic leadership and commitment to community policing, Shavies has led complex investigations, managed high-profile events, and implemented forward-thinking crime prevention and engagement strategies. “Piedmont is incredibly fortunate to welcome Frederick Shavies as our next Chief of Police,” said Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. “He brings exceptional law enforcement experience, a strong commitment to equity and accountability, and a proven ability to lead with integrity. His familiarity with our community and ability to build trust make him the right person to lead the department into its next chapter.” Frederick Shavies began as Piedmont’s new Chief of Police on July 22.

Lessons from those events—and recent fires across California—are clear: when residents actively manage the vegetation around their homes, communities are better protected. • Wildfire prep starts at home: Piedmont urges residents to prune trees, clear debris, and maintain defensible space around homes. • City is at work: Crews deploy goats, clear brush, and trim street trees as part of year-round fire prevention efforts. • Help is available: Free yard inspections and wildfire safety resources are offered at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. Tips for preparing your yard While the gold standard is to clear all vegetation within five feet of your home, even small steps can improve your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire. It is important to remember that the stories of the Bible are more enduring than our interpretations of them, no matter how “kid-friendly” our interpretations may be; that the narratives of the Scripture far outshine our explanations of them, no matter how theologically profound our explanations are. There is comfort in this. If we can just tell the stories, the stories will do their life-shaping work. They will get into the heads, hearts and minds of the leaders as well as the young people, the teachers, as well as the students. We who lead don’t have to be experts in Bible, theology, or child psychology, we simply need, gently and humbly, to give voice to the stories. This is especially true on Thursdays, the day most curriculums focus on the death and resurrection of Jesus. While I personally struggle with interpretations that suggest Jesus’ crucifixion was a price he paid for our sins, for others such interpretations are life giving and inspiring. Conversely, I am drawn to interpretations of the crucifixion that suggest it is a portrayal of the depths to which God suffers with us. For others, such interpretations are overly vague and abstract. In this regard it is important to note that historically Christianity as a whole has never been able to develop an explanation of the meaning and significance of Jesus’ death so satisfactory that it has been declared to be the final word on the matter. Still, it tells the story. It is equally important to note that when children hear the accounts of the crucifixion they are far less interested in its theological interpretations than in the crown of thorns, the nails, the cross and the cries of Jesus. Working for the paper has given me some truly incredible opportunities and opened up some wonderful conIf I’d never started to deliver papers, I would not have had the courage to submit an article about my Scout troop’s weekend outing at Kirby Cove. The article was sent to someone I am now proud to call not only my boss, but a treasured friend – Mr. Gray Gray has become one of my greatest supporters and helped me once more on my scouting journey when he sponsored me for the 2023 National Jamboree. Additionally, he allowed me to put pamphlets into the papers in order to fundraise further. Forever supportive of my writing and praising my articles, I do not believe my experience with the Post would have been half as enjoyable without his continued engagement. In the way you smile at the other kids picking up their papers or folding them on the benches. And finally, delivering for the Post has taught me so much, not only in the literal sense of responsibility and what it means to have people depend on you, but also more indirectly. It’s helped me sharpen my soft skills in striking up conversation and writing emails. Truly, it’s helped me communicate better overall. The depths of my gratitude to the Post have no end, but I would like to try and humbly recognize just how incredible their impact has been on me. Thank you for all you have done, Piedmont Post. articles.text: Editor: I think I speak for most in the community when I express my joy that there are now bald eagles taking residence in Piedmont. I humbly request a few safety considerations: Risk to pets: According to the Raptor Project, bald eagles can carry more than their body weight — one bald eagle was found to have carried an object weighing 12 pounds. But this doesn’t mean we need to put leashes or harnesses on our cats; rather keep an eye on them. Risk to ecosystem: bald eagles do not harm the environment, but their presence could create a competitive challenge against other birds of prey like local hawk species; and could pose a danger to small mammals like squirrels. Consider closing the lids to your compost bins so that animals displaced by the eagles don’t forage in your refuse. In summary, bald eagles represent freedom, strength and independence; may we enjoy these birds and be reminded of their grandeur. –Jay Bohanion

articles.text: On Monday, September 1, Children’s Fairyland turns 75 and will celebrate with a full day of family fun from 10 a.m.- 4 p.m. The Labor Day event will feature performances by DJ Lance Rock, Prescott Circus, and Daisy the Clown, with hands-on activities, interactive art, a brand-new bilingual puppet show, giveaways, special guests, and a parade through Oakland. “This isn’t just a birthday party, it’s our love letter to the generations of families that have supported Children’s Fairyland,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Fairyland. “For 75 years, Fairyland has been a place where kids and families fall in love with storytelling, make cherished memories, and feel safe to play, explore, and connect. This celebration honors our past, reflects on our growth, and opens a new chapter in Fairyland’s story.” The 75th Birthday Party kicks off at 9:30 a.m. with a Parade to the Birthday Party, co-hosted by BART and Fairyland. Starting at the 19th Street BART Station, the parade winds its way to Lake Merritt and ends at the Fairy Gates. DJ L a nce Ro ck , t he Emmy-nominated host of the hit Nick Jr. Series “Yo Gabba Gabba!,” brings his signature mix of music, storytelling, and dance to Fairyland’s Festival Stage. He’ll perform live twice, at 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m., each followed by a meet and greet. The birthday party will also premiere “Tío Conejo’s Big Wish,” Fairyland’s first fully bilingual puppet show based on a folktale from Cuba. The show will run through October 26th, with daily performances at 11:00 a.m., 2:00 p.m., and 4:00 p.m. A live show by Prescott Circus at noon will feature Oakland youth performers showcasing acrobatics and juggling. A bubble-filled performance by Daisy the Clown at 2:30 p.m., blending balloon twisting, magic, and playful chaos. Daisy is a beloved performer known for creating interactive and creative fun for kids of all ages. Puppet Playdates with Quercus, Fairyland’s fuzzy mascot, occur at 11:20 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. Children’s Theatre interactive performances of “Teddy Bear’s Wish” start at 11:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. The activities include art stations, a giant birthday card for Fairyland, a community-painted mural, and a Birthday Adventure Passport activity, where kids collect stamps after completing activities and prompts, then turn it in for a limited-edition 75th anniversary button. All kids will take home special goodie bags. Children’s Fairyland opened its gates on September 2, 1950 as the country’s first storybook theme park, built specifically for young children. Fairyland quickly became a cherished part of Oakland’s identity and cultural landscape, igniting imaginations, shaping childhoods, and inspiring countless theme parks around the world. The idea for creating a storybook theme park in Oakland began in 1948, when local nursery owner Arthur Navlet envisioned a place where children could play freely and safely through a world built just for them. With support from the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Oakland Parks Superintendent William Penn Mott Jr., and a dedicated group of community members, the dream for Children’s Fairyland took shape. Since then, Fairyland has remained a cherished part of Oakland’s cultural landscape, attracting nearly 200,000 visitors annually to explore the park’s 10 acres. Over the years, it has grown to include cultural celebrations, literacy programs, puppet education, summer camps, and one-of-a-kind performances that reflect the diverse cultural heritage of the Bay Area. The park has remained true to its roots over the decades, providing hands-on, screen-free experiences that inspire imagination, creativity, confidence, and a lifelong love of learning. Buy tickets in advance at Fairyland.org Celebrate 75 years of Fairyland on Labor Day, September 1.

articles.text: The usage and possession of smartphones and other mobile communication devices on school grounds remained a hot topic for much of last school year as Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) sought to comply with Assembly Bill 3216, the Phone-Free Schools Act. In Piedmont next year, only high school students will be permitted to use cell phones, and only: before school, after school and during lunch. A full ban of smartphones and mobile communication devices is planned for 2026-27 year. The statewide bill requires school districts to adopt, by July 1, 2026, “a policy to limit or prohibit the use by its pupils of smartphones while the pupils are at a school site.” During the May 28 school board meeting, board members gave their final thoughts before the district approved Board Policy 5131.8. “I hope that we are going to be innovative and think about the culture change of this in our implementation,” said board member Susy Struble. “To me the biggest issue here is the distraction and the lessening of our kids’ ability to have deep focus and pay attention.” A Cell Phone Task Force was assembled in 2024 including parents, and staff from every school site. The task force met on multiple occasions between December 2024 and February 2025 to explore research, consult other districts, and draft policy options; they then presented an update to the board on March 12. “Student input has been an important part of our cell phone policy development,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “I met with middle and high school students last year, including invitations to participate in a survey and to join our cell phone workshop. The Board and I also met with the journalism class in the spring to hear additional feedback about how to engage more students. Next year, I plan to hold several meetings in the fall for students and parents to continue to gather feedback on the policy.” For the 2025-26 school year the policy states “Smartphones and other mobile communication devices shall not be used in any manner that infringes on the privacy rights of any other person. • Primary and middle school students shall have their personal devices off, or silenced, and stored during the instructional day. • High School students shall have their phones, smartphones, and smart devices turned off, or silenced, during instructional time unless instructed by a school administrator, or teacher or authorized by the district. High School Students shall be able to use their devices before school, during lunch, and after school.” The district’s decision comes amid a broader national shift toward phone-free schools. In California, Assembly Bill 3216 reflects growing concern about the impact of device use on student focus, mental health, and classroom behavior. Several districts, including Los Angeles Unified and San Mateo Union High School District, have already adopted stricter phone policies ahead of the state’s July 2026 compliance deadline. Piedmont’s policy includes the following four exceptions for student device use. 1. In the case of an emergency, or in response to a perceived threat of danger; 2. When a teacher or administrator grants permission to the student to possess or use a mobile communication device, subject to any reasonable limitation imposed by that teacher or administrator; 3. When a licensed physician or surgeon determines that the possession or use is necessary for the student’s health and well-being; 4. When the possession or use is required by the student’s individualized education program. The policy received a lengthy first reading discussion during the school board meeting on May 14, which included some dissenting opinions from parents and students. The meeting’s recording is available at Piedmont.granicus. com/player/clip/3069?view_ id=9&redirect=true When school starts up in 19 days, on August 11, there will certainly be a learning curve for students to adjust to the new policy, and for staff on how to enforce the policy. “One thing I learned was that we have policies in place that are not consistently enforced,” said board member Ruchi Medhekar. “The fact that there is a difference from classroom to classroom, from grade to grade, to me, is not in the spirit of the existing policy.” Medhekar also spoke out against teachers giving “device time” as a reward for finishing work early. Board member Max Roman put some of the onus on the board itself to help with the small changes next year and bigger changes a year away. “We could do a better job at creating spaces and things for kids to do, at passing and lunch periods, where they now tend to look at their phones,” said Roman. “I actually suspect that the kids will end up rediscovering the joy of talking to each other with their faces,” added Roman.

articles.text: A March 27 decision by Piedmont School Board and the high school athletic director Tyler Small to not bring back 17-year veteran Girls’ Soccer Head Coach, Dan Chubbock received lengthy criticism during the April 23 school board meeting. The issue was not included on the meeting’s agenda, so a line of soccer players and parents paraded to the microphone to speak out against the decision during public comment for items not on the agenda. “I want to address the abrupt firing of our coach and set the record straight on him.” said Darcy McKee, a junior and a captain of the team. “His team talks are a perfect balance of expectation and encouragement. It is so motivating to see how invested he is in our every performance.” “I was planning to play soccer again next season as a junior with coach Dan and the team, but with this recent decision, I am unsure if I will be playing,” said Chloe Toyama. “[Chubbock] always brought positivity, laughter and a competitive spirit that pushed us to grow and succeed,” added Ellia Kwan. The many comments of praise also introduced another thread of emotion – the shock and frustration of another Athletic Director, Tyler Small, for making such an unpopular decision In his first year as AD. Piedmont parent, PHS alum, and Piedmont Soccer Club board member Jonathan Essner asked the school board to handle situations like these with more grace, respect and professionalism. “Dan was fired from his role in a three-minute phone call with the athletic director. I was taken aback, left to think something egregious had taken place given the unceremonious nature of the dismissal,” said Essner. “For Tyler to not rehire Dan for the poor atmosphere on girls’ soccer, without consulting anyone on the team about [the] atmosphere is wrong and he (Small) has made a mistake,” said senior Ava Sauer. “Compounded with his many scheduling errors all season erodes my faith in Tyler as an athletic director.” Tim Lasocki, a girls soccer parent and the President of the Piedmont Soccer Club reminded the school board that two years the PHS girls soccer team and Chubbock were coach were honored in City Hall for winning sectionals and a day in their honor was created. “The athletic director, Tyler 17-year veteran Girls’ Soccer Head Coach Dan Chubbock was let go after this year. Small, collected no feedback from players or families before releasing the 17-year head coach of the program,” said Lasocki. School board members sat and listened to 17 minutes of rebuke from the soccer community but did not respond under provisions of California’s Brown Act. The job posting for Chubbock’s post is still active and can be seen at Edjoin.org/Home/JobPosting/2065995. “[Girls soccer] was not broken, but it could be now,” said soccer parent and videographer Neil McKee.

PUSD cell phone policy for students By Jay Russell The usage and possession of smartphones and other mobile communication devices on school grounds remained a hot topic for much of last school year as Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) sought to comply with Assembly Bill 3216, the Phone-Free Schools Act. In Piedmont next year, only high school students will be permitted to use cell phones, and only: before school, after school and during lunch. A full ban of smartphones and mobile communication devices is planned for 2026-27 year. The statewide bill requires school districts to adopt, by July 1, 2026, “a policy to limit or prohibit the use by its pupils of smartphones while the pupils are at a school site.” During the May 28 school board meeting, board members gave their final thoughts before the district approved Board Policy 5131.8. “I hope that we are going to be innovative and think about the culture change of this in our implementation,” said board member Susy Struble. “To me the biggest issue here is the distraction and the lessening of our kids’ ability to have deep focus and pay attention.” A Cell Phone Task Force was assembled in 2024 including parents, and staff from every school site. The task force met on multiple occasions between December 2024 and February 2025 to explore research, consult other districts, and draft policy options; they then presented an update to the board on March 12. “Student input has been an important part of our cell phone policy development,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “I met with middle and high school students last year, including invitations to participate in a survey and to join our cell phone workshop. The Board and I also met with the journalism class in the spring to hear additional feedback about how to engage more students. Next year, I plan to hold several meetings in the fall for students and parents to continue to gather feedback on the policy.” For the 2025-26 school year the policy states “Smartphones and other mobile communication devices shall not be used in any manner that infringes on the privacy rights of any other person. • Primary and middle school students shall have their personal devices off, or silenced, and stored during the instructional day. • High School students shall have their phones, smartphones, and smart devices turned off, or silenced, during instructional time unless instructed by a school administrator, or teacher or authorized by the district. High School Students shall be able to use their devices before school, during lunch, and after school.” The district’s decision comes amid a broader national shift toward phone-free schools. In California, Assembly Bill 3216 reflects growing concern about the impact of device use on student focus, mental health, and classroom behavior. Several districts, including Los Angeles Unified and San Mateo Union High School District, have already adopted stricter phone policies ahead of the state’s July 2026 compliance deadline. Piedmont’s policy includes the following four exceptions for student device use. 1. In the case of an emergency, or in response to a perceived threat of danger; 2. When a teacher or administrator grants permission to the student to possess or use a mobile communication device, subject to any reasonable limitation imposed by that teacher or administrator; 3. When a licensed physician or surgeon determines that the possession or use is necessary for the student’s health and well-being; 4. When the possession or use is required by the student’s individualized education program. The policy received a lengthy first reading discussion during the school board meeting on May 14, which included some dissenting opinions from parents and students. The meeting’s recording is available at Piedmont.granicus. com/player/clip/3069?view_ id=9&redirect=true When school starts up in 19 days, on August 11, there will certainly be a learning curve for students to adjust to the new policy, and for staff on how to enforce the policy. “One thing I learned was that we have policies in place that are not consistently enforced,” said board member Ruchi Medhekar. “The fact that there is a difference from classroom to classroom, from grade to grade, to me, is not in the spirit of the existing policy.” Medhekar also spoke out against teachers giving “device time” as a reward for finishing work early. Board member Max Roman put some of the onus on the board itself to help with the small changes next year and bigger changes a year away. “We could do a better job at creating spaces and things for kids to do, at passing and lunch periods, where they now tend to look at their phones,” said Roman. “I actually suspect that the kids will end up rediscovering the joy of talking to each other with their faces,” added Roman.

articles.text: In June 2025 a team of high schoolers led by Piedmont Community Service Crew member Nathan Bekele embarked on a three-week journey to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, partnering with St. Paul’s Hospital and Melu’e Foundation, one of the country’s few autism centers. The group’s goal was to raise awareness, deliver supplies, and provide hands-on support for children with developmental disabilities. The trip began with strong community support, centered around the “Taste of Ethiopia” at Lemat Restaurant in Berkeley. It raised $35,000 through ticket sales and a lively art auction featuring Ethiopian artists, including one who grew up at Melu’e Foundation. Reflecting on the challenge and growth of volunteering abroad, Piedmont High School student Kidus Yalew shared, “Going to Ethiopia was a hard challenge, but it showed me that even far from home, friendship can feel like family. We spent our days helping out at the hospital and spending time with autistic kids. I saw how just being there for others can bring hope, even on the tough days. I realized resilience isn’t about handling everything on your own, it’s about serving together, leaning on each other, and finding strength in community.” Funds from the fundraiser helped pay six months’ rent for Melu’e Foundation and supplied essential therapy equipment, computers, furniture, and care packages for pediatric oncology units at St. Paul’s Hospital and Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital (Black Lion Hospital). During the trip, while shadowing under doctors in the ICU at St. Paul’s Hospital, the team came across a 16-year-old girl diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome. Her condition was rapidly worsening, and the medicine needed to stabilize her was far beyond her family’s financial reach. Moved by the urgency of the situation, the team took immediate action by texting their donor support group in the U.S. and raising $3,000 in a single afternoon to cover the full cost Chloe Park (left), TJ Park, Amanuel Girma, Lucas Bekele, Nathan Bekele, Ethan Mesfin, Joaquin Fierro, Theodros Girma, Gabriella Mesfin, and Kidus Yalew of her life-saving treatment. The experience became a defining moment of the trip, highlighting the impact of compassion, quick action, and community support in saving lives. Coronado High School student Gabriella Mesfin, a relative of Bekele, described the emotional impact of working directly with the children. “Working with the children was a meaningful experience. One moment that stood out was seeing their joy during our time together. This cause matters because it brings hope to those in need. Helping raise $3,000 for the 16-year-old showed me how powerful community support can be,” she said. The team’s efforts received national coverage on Ethiopian television, reaching tens of thousands of viewers and helping break the stigma around autism in the country. The trip concluded with a final ceremony, where Bekele, local hospital leaders, and nonprofit directors emphasized the ongoing commitment to autism advocacy. This initiative demonstrates how young people can foster meaningful change through cross-cultural partnerships, compassion, and perseverance—lessons that will continue to inspire all involved for years to come. At Chabot Space & Science Center, we spend these nights gazing into the cosmos and invite you to do the same. Whether you’re looking through a telescope or simply lying back to watch the stars, this season is perfect for connecting with the universe while spending time with the “astronomer next door”. The Ring Nebula: A star’s last breath A highlight of the summer sky is the Ring Nebula, a beautiful remnant of a dying star in the constellation Lyra. Look for Lyra high in the eastern sky around 9:00PM. Its brightest star, Vega, glows bluish-white and points the way to the Ring Nebula. Though invisible to the naked eye, you can see it through our observatory telescopes or with your own, available in our gift shop! The Ring Nebula lies 2,500 light-years away. Unlike explosive supernovae, most stars end their lives slowly. After billions of years, they expand into red giants, shedding their outer gas layers over thousands of years. What remains is a white dwarf: a hot, dense stellar core. The radiation from this core lights up the gas, forming a glowing cloud we call a planetary nebula. Pogačar won Stage 4 to put himself in second place and then regained the Yellow Jersey the following day in a 33-km time trial. Piedmont High School senior Layth Haddawy has quickly ascended up the rankings entering the third year of his competitive powerlifting career. On July 8 he won the U.S. Powerlifting National Championship in Las Vegas in the age 16-17 category. Haddawy lifted a combined total of 1,118 pounds, including 380 pounds in the squat, 253.5 pounds on the bench press, and a 485 pound dead lift. Haddawy won in a field of three, receiving a score of 395.87 and beating the second-place lifter by 58 points. “I am very proud of this achievement and feel gratified in knowing that I was able to compete in a more competitive division than last year and manage to place better,” Haddawy said. Layth last competed in the USPA Get Bent’s Spring Break in Oakland on April 5 where he lifted 1,085 total pounds. Three months later, Haddawy increased his squat by 28 pounds and his bench by 5.5 pounds. Haddawy hit three reps in the squats at the 2025 National Championship, increasing his weight each time by lifting 341 pounds, 363 pounds, and finishing by jumping 17 pounds to 380. “When I first started powerlifting, my squat had been the lift that I had the least experience with out of the three. So over the last year, I have put far more effort into improving my squat. The large jumps among the three reps were because I was conserving energy for the last rep,” Haddawy said. At last year’s USPA National Championship, Haddawy finished second in a field of 10, but he later learned he was dealing with a fracture in his pelvis. An MRI revealed Layth suffered an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. He spent the following months rehabbing and training for his next event in April 2025. articles.text: Staff Photos Tanya Kononova graduated from Piedmont High School in 2024 and competed on the Highlanders’ tennis team for two years after coming to Piedmont as a Ukrainian refugee. [Updated from August 2022] Tanya Kononova graduated from Piedmont High with the Class of 2024 and made a big name for herself as a standout tennis star, earning the Western Alameda County Conference’s Player of the Year award in 2022 as a junior after winning the league’s individual tournament’s singles bracket while she finished second the following year. She just finished her freshman year at San Diego State. Her path from Europe to the Highlanders’ tennis team wasn’t the typical journey like foreign exchange students who come to Piedmont High. For Tanya and her family, they never envisioned staying in California as a refugee prior to February 24, 2022—the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived to Piedmont on July 22 of 2022 from Odesa, a city on the southern shore of Ukraine. Kononova turned up to coach Jim Landes’ tennis clinic a week later, instantly impressing him. “It was the week I had the high school girls warm up clinic, one week before tryouts. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. Right then and there, I knew she was a very good player the first time she hit. That was a good warm up for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Departing from her country is an unimaginable experience to those of us here tucked away in the hills. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russians invaded. Her father is still in Ukraine as men under the age of 60-years old were kept from leaving the country. She stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months and was forced to wait at the border for 13 hours before passing into the neighboring country. She described the experience of leaving Ukraine. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova when speaking through a translator. Tanya and her family then decided to relocate to Bulgaria from May through July 2022 after a town administration building nearby in Moldova was targeted by Russian artillery. They had no connection to anyone in the country, forced to forge their own way. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived with me, my mother, my grandfather and my grandmother,” said Kononova. When initially leaving Odesa, she and her family were forced to quickly throw together their belongings because of fear that the Russians would siege the city. They only grabbed two suitcases with just some items to get by, like some clothes, textbooks, and her cell phone before making their way to Moldova.
articles.title: Tanya Kononova details her journey as a Ukrainian refugee and Piedmont tennis player

articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team, a yearsound organization, will host tryouts on August 19-21 at Montclair Swim Club, 1901 Woodhaven Way. Tryouts will be from 4:00- 6:30 pm on all three days. Swimmers will be grouped by age and given a 30-minute time slot. The coaching staff expects that swimmers (ages 9 and over) to be available on all three days to get a clear sense of swim competency and coachability, which will help with group placement. Swimmers ages 8 and under are only expected to come for two days, August 19-20. PST is comprised of eight swim groups (Green, Blue, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, YRHS (year-round high school) and Titanium). For more information about the expectations of the differing groups, please refer to the PST 2025-2026 Handbook found on the website at the bottom of the article. Please note that PST is a yearround swim team (see exception below*). This tryout is for the 2025-2026 swim season. Practices for all accepted swimmers will begin on 8/23/25. For families joining PST in our younger groups, Green and Blue only, we realize the commitment to a competitive swim team might not be fully appreciated. As a way to support and encourage new swimmers to discover their love for swimming, PST will offer shorter terms for Green group families (12 weeks in the fall, 12 weeks in the spring, and 8 weeks in the summer). You can register for the fall session only or choose to continue on. The Blue group will have a 6-month trial that runs August to February. In January, Blue group swimmers and their guardian(s) will meet with their swim coach and decide if PST’s competitive swim program is the correct environment for their swimmer to thrive. Swimmers in the Blue group can opt to leave the team in February or continue on. This family trial is only available to swimmers who are new to PST and who participate in our Blue group. articles.text: In this week of Hiking with Jon we delve into our fourth of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe, to include one of the tallest peaks in California, Washeshu Peak (formerly Squaw Peak) at Palisades Tahoe in Olympic Valley. If you are in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a hike with a million-dollar view atop Washeshu Peak at over 8,000 feet in elevation. Palisades Tahoe Olympic Valley is a popular destination for Piedmont residents on ski week. But during the summer months, the region becomes a prime hiking location with wildflowers and sweeping awe striking views of Lake Tahoe and Desolation Wilderness. The resort and mountain peak was previously changed from “Squaw Valley” and “Squaw Peak” following extensive research into the Washoe Tribe history, whose ancestral lands were in Olympic Valley. Washeshu is in commemoration of the Washoe Tribe. Early literature from the tribe indicates the term Wa She Shu translates to “People from here.” Our day starts by taking the aerial tram ride up to High Camp, which gives another incredible view from the viewing platform back towards Lake Tahoe, a popular restaurant, outdoor games, a skating rink, and Olympic museum dedicated to the 1960 Winter Games. The large-scale pool and hot tub, unfortunately, has remained closed for several years due to extensive repairs. From High Camp, walking to Washeshu Peak is a two-mile straight shot and around 850 feet in elevation gain with the final 0.6 of a mile to the peak provides the sharpest ascent. The trail averages less than 10 percent gradient for the first 1.3 miles before making the climb to Washeshu Peak. At the 1.3 mile mark, hikers will come to a junction with a path on the left shooting upwards towards the Staff Photos The view from Washeshu Peak towards Lake Tahoe. articles.text: Dolly Parton The San Francisco Symphony, joined by a cast of guest vocalists and musicians, will perform hit songs by iconic country pop music star Dolly Parton in a special multimedia concert on Friday, August 1 entitled Dolly Parton’s Threads: My Songs In Symphony. The innovative and unique concert features the country legend on screen, leading audiences in a visual-musical biopic and through key highlights of her storied sixty-year career. Symphony musicians will play alongside solo artists including vocalists Hollie Hammel, Julie Williams and Katelyn Drye; guitarists Derek Drye, Lindsey Miller, Dean Berner; bassist Gary Lunn, and percussionist Chris Leidhecker. Conductor Jack Everly, principal conductor of the Indianapolis Symphony and the Naples Philharmonic, leads the artists and San Francisco Symphony featuring Parton’s hit songs “Jolene,” “Coat Of Many Colors,” “I Will Always Love You,” and more. Parton is one of only a handful of individuals to receive at least one nomination from all four major annual American entertainment award organizations, including an Emmy, GRAMMY, Oscar, and Tony. Her career spans 60 years and 49 albums, and her music has influenced generations of pop, country, blues and soul recording artists. She also founded a number of charitable and philanthropic organizations, including the Dollywood Foundation which brings education and poverty relief to her hometown in east Tennessee. All songs performed at the Dolly Parton’s Threads: My Songs In Symphony concert are written by Parton unless otherwise noted. Orchestral arrangements are by David Hamilton. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/SWTS25-Dolly-Parton to purchase tickets, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. Tickets are limited.

articles.text: Korsa Musical Theater, a Bay Area musical theater training company, concludes its 20th season with a production of Oklahoma! at the Pinole Valley High School Theater. Tickets are available for three more performances, including two 7 p.m. performances on July 25 and 26; and a 2 p.m. matinee on July 28. Oklahoma! is the first musical written by Rodgers and Hammerstein, a theater-writing team of composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist-dramatist Oscar Hammerstein II. The 1943 musical is based on Lynn Riggs’s 1931 play Green Grow the Lilacs and follows the story of farmgirl Laurey and cowboy Curly’s budding romance, threatened by a brooding ranch-hand named Jud. The play ran for over five years on Broadway, a record that would not be bested until My Fair Lady’s initial run in 1956. Korsa Musical Theater’s production features a cast of 33 student performers age 13 through 20, led by a team of professional directors including award-winning Director Susannah Martin, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Janet Collard. The production also includes a 30-piece live orchestra, with five student instrumentalists playing Robert Russell Bennet’s original score. Tickets are available online at www.korsamt.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $18–$40, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. Pinole Valley High School Theater is located at 2900 Pinole Valley Road in Pinole. articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe is playing onstage now through August 10. The one-woman stage show The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe was originally written by Jane Wagner and turned into a critically-acclaimed film in 1991. The show is often praised, and considered controversial at the time, for its feminist material including the compressed history of the feminist movement offered in Act 2. Writer and comedian Marga Gomez stars in Wagner’s iconic play as Trudy, an eccentric bag lady who serves as a bridge between Earth and the cosmos. The protagonist becomes a whole cast of comedic, quirky characters, weaving together tales of a punk-rock rebel, wealthy Californian socialites, and feminist reactionaries. “There are so many Signs of Stupid Life in 2025 that I am excited to revive this iconic play to experience something way more intelligent,” Gomez shared. “I first saw [the play] on Broadway when I was hitting open mics and working odd jobs. I was Marga Gomez in Aurora’s The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe awed. I had goosebumps. If anyone told me back then I would be performing Jane and Lily’s iconic characters someday I would have freaked out.” Gomez is an acclaimed comedian known for her dynamic storytelling and brings her unique voice to this one-woman tour de force. She is the recipient of the GLAAD Media Award for Theatre. “I couldn’t be more thrilled to see Marga Gomez stepping in to Lily Tomlin’s iconic role,” said Josh Costello, Aurora’s Artistic Director. “Anyone who has seen Marga perform knows she is a Bay Area treasure. There has always been a connection between Lily Tomlin’s work and Marga’s, so it’s fitting that Marga will be the one to perform Search for Signs at Aurora.” Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/search-for-signs for showtimes and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Event is part of TIM’s free public programs Author Liz Schott leads a discussion on Dorothy Wright Liebes’ legacy and involvement in the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition this Saturday, July 26, at Treasure Island Museum. The event is part of the museum’s free summer programming that aims to inform residents and visitors of the island’s historical relevance. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, July 23, 2025 MOVIES FOR ADULTS 1917 – Remembering World War I By Chris Honoré Before discussing writer/ director Sam Mendes’ film 1917, I feel I would be remiss not to mention Peter Jackson’s extraordinary They Will Not Grow Old. He was given access to hundreds of archival WWI news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum – scratched, grainy, and hand cranked film that he, using state-of-the-art restorative technology, not only colorized but literally brought back to life. It’s as if he opened a portal in time and we see young Brits gathered on a battlefield, waiting, some, breaking the fourth wall, staring into the camera, smiling, their youthful faces filled with an optimistic eagerness that would soon be devastatingly transformed. WWI, which began in July of 1914 and lasted until November or 1918, was one of the deadliest wars in history. Nine million combatants and seven million civilians were killed as a direct result. Indirectly, 50 to 100 million deaths occurred worldwide, attributed to what was referred to as the “Spanish Flu,” the pandemic thought to have begun in the damp, muddy, disease-ridden trenches, conditions that were almost as lethal as the withering machinegun fire, shelling and chlorine gas faced by the troops. WWI was an extraordinary display of nationalistic hubris, bordering on a collective insanity in which millions of men, on all sides, were sacrificed for mere yards of soil. It was a nightmare of George MacKay stars in 1917 the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. The story is deceptively simple: two young soldiers – Lance Corporal Schofield (George McKay) and Lance Corporal Blake (Dean Charles Chapman) – are ordered by their general to deliver a letter to a command post some eight miles away, instructing the commanding officer to stand his troops (two battalions, numbering 1,600 men) down. They are told that all lines of communication have been cut. The intelligence in the letter explains that the Germans have fashioned a trap and should the dawn assault take place, casualties will be grave. The caveat is that to arrive at the command post, the distance to be crossed is, in truth, a No Man’s Land, comprised of German troops (thought to have retreated), desiccated terrain and trenches. The general adds that among the battalions waiting is Corporal Blake’s brother. And so, the two climb up a ladder onto the lip of a deep trench, urging one another on, Schofield expressing his reluctance, yet both feeling the urgency of their mission. What they leave behind are green fields and wildflowers; it’s a beautiful spring afternoon in April. But what they find as they move ever deeper into enemy territory is a landscape of utter destruction – deep craters filled with water and bodies, dead horses, stretching barbed wire, and a horror of mud, death and unrecognizable carrion covered with flies and feeding birds. Hell has been there and left. Their sense of urgency is palpable; to fail would be catastrophic; they must survive in order to deliver the letter carried inside Corporal Blake’s tunic. Any hint of exposition – backstory, shared memories of origin or tales of home – is inconsequential. What we hear are the sounds of their breathing, the rasp and clank of their gear as Blake and Schofield crouch forward, bayoneted rifles ever at the ready. This is the narrative arc. However, what writer/director Sam Mendes and legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins do, from the outset, is create the illusion that the camera is the third person on the journey and the entire film is shot in one long take, never cutting away. Of course, that is not the case, but the impact of this most effective photographic technique (not a conceit) is striking. In other words, 1917 is a truly visual film, and it is the camera that propels it forward, Blake and Schofield moving constantly, the story revealed as they grimly survey all that is before them. And so, the question posed is: can Mendes and Deakins capture and then sustain the attention of the audience as the fraught images escalate, the faces of the two made grimly fearful by what they witness, leaving them to wonder what, among all this carnage, awaits them. I would judge that 1917 is an engaging, photographic marvel and a marvelous achievement, possessing a wonderful score by Thomas Newman and truly fine performances by both MacKay and Chapman. 1917. articles.text: Sophie and the Rising Sun is set in a small coastal South Carolina town named Salty Creek. It’s autumn, and the year is 1941. The film opens with a bus stopping brief ly and leaves behind a semi-conscious, injured man lying in the grass near the bus stop. A number of locals who witnessed this unexpected moment gather around the man and notice that he is Asian and assume he is, to use their word, a “Chinaman.” Someone leans down and asks him his name. The man struggles to whisper, “Ohta.” Perplexed, uncertain as to what to do with the man, three prominent townsmen approach long-time resident Ann Morrison (Margo Martindale) who is recently widowed and has a cottage behind her house, currently being used for gardening supplies. Explaining that the man needs a place to recover they ask her if he might stay in her cottage. Out of concern and generosity, she agrees and understanding that Mr. Ohta (Takashi Yamaguchi) will need care has her maid begin to look after him. And so the story begins to unfold. We soon learn that living next to Mrs. Morrison is a young woman, Sophie Willis. She lost her husband in WWI, and now supports herself by fishing lobsters just off the coast during the week, and on Sundays, carrying her easel and paints, captures on canvas the ocean and the surrounding wildlife. Slowly Mr. Ohta begins to mend and reveals not only his quiet decency, but his skills as a gardener, a talent that surprises and pleases Mrs. Morrison for she too finds refuge in simply caring for her plants. Of course, Sophie and Mr. Ohta meet and she discovers that he shares her love of painting and their paths cross each Sunday morning. What changes the warm, heartfelt arc of the narrative is December 7, 1941. Mr. Ohta tells Ann that he is not Chinese but Japanese and was born in America. The townspeople of Salty Creek initially react to the presence of Mr. Ohta with curiosity and even suspicion, with the attack on Pearl Harbor ot soon emerges as gossipy, racist and xenophobic with the exception of Ann, her newly hired maid Salomé (Lorraine Toussaint), and Sophie. These women soon begin to comprehend the risk involved for Mr. Ohta should he remain in Salty Creek. Sophie and the rising Sun is not only an exceptionally fine film, with strong performances (look for Margo Martindale). At this moment it is also timely. Sophie and the Rising Sun. articles.text: Gerard Butler and Jonny Weston in Chasing Mavericks Chasing Mavericks is a family friendly, classic sports story, reminiscent of those inspirational films that were so ubiquitous in the 70s and 80s. The field of play, however, is not a grassy pitch or an oval track; rather, it’s based on a true story set in a famous surfing spot, just north of Half Moon Bay, Ca., known for its monster-size 30 foot waves (some peaking over 60 feet) and a dangerous, life threatening undertow. It’s called Mavericks. The focus of the film is a teenager, Jay Moriarity (Johnny Weston), whose dream is to ride the seemingly impossible northern Pacific break. He quickly learns that to ride and survive the El Nino created waves will require not only extensive training and endurance, but the ability to hold one’s breath for some four minutes or risk drowning. The narrative opens with 9-year-old Jay attempting to rescue the small dog of his childhood friend, Kim (later portrayed by Leven Rambin), that has has fallen into the surf. Jay is saved from the surging waves by a crusty old surfer, Frosty Hesson (Gerard Butler), who years later reluctantly agrees to mentor Jay, after he persistently shares with Frosty his unyielding desire to surf Mavericks. And so the adventure begins with Frosty putting Jay through a rigorous training regime, insisting that he must learn not only the basics of big wave riding, but must practice those skills that will help him survive the harrowing, unforgiving waves should he wipeout and find himself in the grip of what’s called the “spin cycle.” Frosty also loans Jay his “big gun” long board, and Jay’s single-parent mom (Elisabeth Shue) buys him a weather radio for his 16th birthday, allowing him to track the storms that produce the huge surf. Of course, after months of practice, the singular storm arrives and Jay’s opportunity presents itself. Mavericks is ready; however, will Jay be ready, and will he be able to master the mythical monsters that form and crash with a Zen-like intensity that must be seen to be believed. Meanwhile, Frosty and Kim stand on shore and watch Jay paddling toward his destiny. Chasing Mavericks. Directed by Curtis Hanson, Michael Apted. Starring Gerard Butler, Johnny Wesson, Elisabeth Shue. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG. Released in 2012. Streaming on Disney+/ Fandango/Prime/Apple.

articles.text: Weekends until August 25, 11–2 p.m. Nepalese Art Exhibit This exhibition brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life—particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. articles.text: Nikola Printz Festival Opera continues its 2025 season with a Salon Series of Sunday afternoon concerts in Piedmont featuring some of the Bay Area’s rising stars and critically acclaimed artists. The concerts will be at Piedmont Center for the Arts on July 27, August 24, and September 28. The series offers intimate, artist-curated performances that highlight rare repertoire and virtuosic collaboration between talented singers and musicians alike. articles.text: On a quiet, winding stretch of Buena Vista Way, perched high in the leafy solitude of the Berkeley Hills, lies a residence so richly steeped in history and architectural splendor that even longtime locals may pass by unaware. Shielded by a stately gate and set among old-growth redwoods and oaks, this Berkeley Landmarked home, known as Hume Cloister, is not simply a house—it is a living artifact, a Gothic revival echo of medieval France brought to life with Californian soul. Located at 2900 Buena Vista Way, the estate defies expectations. While Berkeley is no stranger to idiosyncratic homes or storied pedigrees, the Hume Cloister occupies a category of its own. Built in 1929, the estate was the brainchild of Samuel and Portia Bell Hume, an intellectual power couple whose academic and professional contributions still ripple through the University of California system and beyond. Its design, inspired by a 13th-century monastery the couple visited in Toulouse, France, is the work of noted Bay Area architect John Hudson Thomas, a master of eclectic historical revival styles. The result is a residence that would not feel out of place in the French countryside but instead finds itself gazing across the San Francisco Bay. In its construction and setting, the home is an act of artistic ambition and a deeply personal vision. Samuel Hume, a dramatic literature scholar, art curator, and rare book dealer, spent much of his professional life elevating the cultural landscape of California. He served as a professor at UC Berkeley and as director of the Berkeley Art Museum. His wife, Dr. Portia Bell Hume, was a pioneer in psychiatry and mental health education, notably one of the first women to teach in the medical school at UC Berkeley. Together, they envisioned a sanctuary that would not only serve as a home but also as a space for intellectual reflection, creativity, and retreat. And a sanctuary it is. Sited on more than two-thirds of an acre, the Hume Cloister commands unobstructed panoramic views stretching from the San Mateo Bridge to Mt. Tamalpais and beyond. From the main terrace, the Golden Gate Bridge appears perfectly framed, like a painting made by nature and architecture working in concert. The dramatic elevation provides not just vistas but a sense of quiet serenity, rare commodities in today’s ever-expanding world. The house itself is an architectural narrative told in stone, wood, and wrought iron. Upon entering, visitors are met with the scale and craftsmanship of another era: vaulted ceilings soar 25 feet overhead, while massive fireplaces anchor the living spaces. Wrought-iron chandeliers of cathedral scale cast shadows that evoke a sense of monastic calm. Stone arches and a spiral staircase offer a tactile link to the medieval structures that inspired the Humes nearly a century ago. Thomas’s design placed emphasis on balance between grandeur and intimacy. The grand living room leads to a mezzanine library and office space with commanding views over the bay—a setting easily imagined as the workspace for a scholar of literature, or a psychiatrist drafting the early contours of a mental health curriculum. The library is equipped to house more than 2,000 books, and the view from this elevated perch—particularly during the golden hours of early morning and dusk—is nothing short of meditative. At the heart of the residence lies its most distinctive feature: a cloister-style courtyard, modeled At the heart of the residence lies its cloister-style courtyard, modeled directly after those in European monasteries. directly after those in European monasteries. Lined with arched colonnades and featuring a stone wishing well at its center, the courtyard exemplifies the home’s spiritual and architectural mission. It is a space designed not just for contemplation but for communion—with nature, history, and the self. While the architecture pays tribute to medieval sensibilities, the home’s current iteration is anything but antiquated. The present owner has undertaken a comprehensive 7+ year restoration and modernization effort, preserving the historic character while introducing contemporary amenities. The kitchen features a Wolf range, Sub-Zero refrigerator, and custom millwork beneath a louvered ceiling and skylight— marrying utility and aesthetics in a way that honors both the old and the new. Each of the five en-suite bedrooms has been updated with toptier finishes, including custom tilework, copper showerheads, and heated floors. As real estate in the Bay Area continues to evolve, and as historical preservation faces increasing challenges, the Hume Cloister is a rare and precious reminder: that the past, when thoughtfully preserved and lovingly restored, can inform a richly modern life. It is a living museum, yes, but also a home, warm and welcoming, prepared to host the next chapter in its storied life. Whether for a discerning collector, a lover of history, or simply someone in search of unparalleled peace and beauty above the fray, the Hume Cloister offers a singular opportunity. Walkers explore Bellevue, Sharon Avenue By Dick Carter There was good summer turnout of 40 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk. The group was pleased Monica Katzel was visiting family and walking with them for the first time. She reported that former walker Christine Caliste, who lived and worked with the Katzel family and retired to her native Granada, is well, enjoying retirement, and remembers the walkers fondly. Two streets the group hadn’t walked this year were Bellevue and Sharon Avenues. Bellevue has many beautiful and interesting homes. Sharon was developed by early Piedmonter William Sharon and has some interesting history. The group went up Sierra Avenue to the 217-foot path between 17 and 29 Sierra to Mountain Avenue, then to the street triangle where Bellevue intersects with Mountain. They checked on the island oak in the triangle’s center which replaced a Sequoia last year that had been in this intersection for generations. The oak is native to California, and it is hoped it will thrive in this small island that has no regular source of water. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation raised over $8,000 from neighbors for the tree’s planting and care for at least two years. The group went up Bellevue and came to the front gate of a beautiful mansion that is down a long driveway. From the front yard there is a majestic view of San Francisco. On a past walk late friend and walker Will Adams pointed out that the house was placed on the lot specifically so that the driveway entrance would provide the wonderful view. The walkers climbed to the top of Bellevue and went down the steep Pacific Avenue to Dormidera and Sharon Avenues. At Sharon, the history of its development was shared based on an article by Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi in the society’s magazine. William Sharon was born in 1852 and grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he went to San Francisco and then Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, who was a successful banker and silver mine owner. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt in 1876 and became successful in finance and mining too. He was also elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. The Sharons initially lived in Virginia City, but they wanted their children to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. They built a magnificent three-story house in the middle of their land and called it Casa Montana. With their seven children, Lillian’s mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener they moved into it in 1898. However, in 1914 the new City of Piedmont imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. So, in 1915 the Sharons subdivided their land in a development they called Sharon Terrace. It had 20y lots with frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. Some family members built homes on them, and the driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue. Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later also built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon. Sadly, Windsor demolished Casa Montana in 1936. The mansion was replaced by three homes at 27, 33, and 37 Sharon. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses, those at 235 Mountain and 56 and 52 Sharon, remain on the former Casa Montana property. The group saw where Casa Montana once stood, and the remaining historic homes. The walkers took a side trip up Sharon Court, and by chance long time Piedmont recreation coordinator Janet Epstein and husband George were outside their home. Janet told the walkers about the Piedmont Seniors’ group activities that she has managed since 1996. After the unexpected visit with the Epsteins, the group returned to Sharon Avenue. They went down Sharon’s hill to Mountain and enjoyed a lovely, cloudy view of the Bay Bridge along the way. The group noted the 235 Mountain house that was built in 1912 by a Sharon family member. The group got in some additional steps going up Craig Avenue to Highland before their usual noontime return to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. articles.text: “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically narrowed things down to what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. There was a moment when Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week in order to grab more belongings. She visited a friend at the city center when a rocket struck a building close by. Speaking through a translator, Kononova details the emotions she experienced: “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s where it really hit me… I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. We laughed and didn’t go anywhere, but then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions, and it was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family still lives in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncles’ home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends; one of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” said Kononova. When entering the States last year, it marked the first time Kononova swung a racket since departing her country in February 2022. She began playing tennis when she was six years old and continued at the club level through her teenage years. Playing for Piedmont High helps provide an outlet for Tanya in a foreign place so far from home. “It’s completely different from the places I was at before. But, I think it’s a nice place to stay and it feels like you’re safe here. The people are quite happy to see you… Playing on the team definitely makes me feel like someone stands for me. It feels like you’re not alone and it’s less stressful. It’s more fun,” said Kononova. Kononova then burst onto the scene in the fall of 2022 as Piedmont’s incumbent No. 1 singles starter, showing her fierce style and fiery passion on the courts on Tanya Kononova is a former WACC Champion and competed at No. 1 singles for two years. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s where it really hit me… I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. We laughed and didn’t go anywhere, but then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions, and it was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family still lives in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncles’ home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends; one of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” said Kononova. When entering the States last year, it marked the first time Kononova swung a racket since departing her country in February 2022. She began playing tennis when she was six years old and continued at the club level through her teenage years. Playing for Piedmont High helps provide an outlet for Tanya in a foreign place so far from home. “It’s completely different from the places I was at before. But, I think it’s a nice place to stay and it feels like you’re safe here. The people are quite happy to see you… Playing on the team definitely makes me feel like someone stands for me. It feels like you’re not alone and it’s less stressful. It’s more fun,” said Kononova. Kononova then burst onto the scene in the fall of 2022 as Piedmont’s incumbent No. 1 singles starter, showing her fierce style and fiery passion on the courts on her way to the WACC Singles title. She’s been competing at the tournament level throughout the summer and is set to compete in a Level 4 adult tournament, the Brightwork Open in Moraga from August 8-13. Competing in tournaments to build her ranking is mightily beneficial towards her potential college recruitment. “I’ve been working a lot of time with Tanya. She’s getting better all the time. She played in some junior tournaments; she won a Level 6 tournament, she played three Level 5s and reached the semifinals in one and finals in another. She also played one adult tournament, won the first round and lost the second. She’s going to play one more adult tournament in Moraga next week. As she keeps building her ranking, she’ll get noticed,” said Landes. Tanya has become a main figure of the Piedmont High girls’ tennis program, often attending Landes’ clinics and taking part as an assistant to younger students. “She’s been practicing in my clinics. She’s worked for me in my clinics all summer. Now we’re running the high school girls’ clinics with tryouts coming up. She’s really devoted to tennis,” said Landes. She went undefeated against league opponents in the fall of 2022 on her way to the league title and finished fourth in the D2 NCS Individual Tournament. Layth now plans the next step of his powerlifting career in joining Powerlifting America, which will give him a better chance at landing a position on Team USA. “My plan for the future is to leave the current federation I compete in, USPA, and switch to Powerlifting America. As Chief, Bowers led the Piedmont Police Department in significant investments in technology as a force multiplier, establishing Piedmont’s public safety camera system. He also oversaw expansion of dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978 and the construction of the new 911 Dispatch Center, which is expected to be complete this fall. “When we heard Chief Bowers was retiring, we were immediately moved to express our gratitude and appreciation,” said Jennifer Alderman, representing the Jewish Community of Piedmont. Alderman and others presented Bowers with a specially commissioned piece of art by Bay Area artist Nina Bonos, depicting a hamsa – a traditional Jewish symbol for good fortune, safety and protection for the journey ahead. “I’ve spent many times with Jeremy and previous [City] Administrators going through issues, and it’s his insightfulness, his willingness to make decisions, his open-mindedness that always struck me. Those are criteria of leadership,” said former Police Chief Jeremy Bowers (left) receives a piece of art from representatives of Piedmont’s Jewish community. Piedmont mayor Bob McBain. In terms of accolades, Bowers was the recipient of the Movers of Mountains Award in Public Safety and Community Bridge Building from the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Association of Santa Clara Valley. Earlier this year, Bowers was honored by the San Francisco District Attorney’s office with the Hometown Hero Award for his efforts in community engagement and his work partnering with residents and local schools to address gun violence. “I’ll be honest with you,” said Chief Bowers. “Every day I ask myself if I am doing enough? Every day I have doubts if I’m doing enough for my men and women, or the community, or my peers in the city. I think, quite frankly, that’s been my secret to success. I never feel like I’ve arrived – I always feel like there’s more to give. “Up to my last day here, and probably after my last day here, I’ll be questioning if I did enough – because I care.” Bowers closed with thanks to his wife Tricia and children Jordan, Andre and Anjali. Bowers also expressed confidence in Piedmont’s police staff and incoming leadership with the City’s next police chief, Frederick Shavies. The packed City Council chambers delivered Bowers a heartfelt standing ovation at the end of his speech. As a part of the proclamation, Mayor Betsy Andersen declared July 7, 2025 as “Jeremy Bowers Day.” “Chief Bowers, you’ve done enough,” assured Mayor Andersen. “You’ve arrived.” Where in the World Are We?
